Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (health centres/health posts) in Niger predominantly use paper-based recording for patient data, with nurses handling basic services like immunization, maternal/child care, and curative care. No evidence of routine electronic health records or DHIS2 at point of care; DHIS2 functions as national HMIS for aggregate data management and monitoring, likely from facility paper tallies transcribed at district level. Digital systems piloted in isolated projects: OpenClinic HIS at select district hospitals, computerised maintenance in 3 rural districts (management-focused, not patient records). National E-Sante Strategy (2019-2023) prioritizes rural ICT via connectivity and governance pillars, but rollout remains limited. Barriers include poor electricity/internet, low skills, security/climate risks in 80% rural areas. Gap: National digital ambitions for UHC contrast sharply with rural paper-dominant reality; digital confined to aggregation/pilots, not majority POC use. (187 words)

Confirmed via alternative sources: rural health centres/posts in Niger are staffed by nurses delivering a minimum paper-based service package (Ortuno-Gutierrez et al. 2025); DHIS2 remains the national aggregate HMIS, not a facility point-of-care system (DHIS2/Gavi 2025, OpenHEXA 2025 describing 32+ siloed platforms with DHIS2 hosted at Directorate of Statistics level). A new community-health mHealth digital tool is being rolled out to 4 of 8 regions (Jan 2026) for structured monitoring of under-5s/mothers, but this targets community health worker home visits rather than confirmed routine digital data capture inside rural clinics themselves, so it does not yet establish facility-level digitisation. Score of Entirely paper confirmed; worth revisiting as mHealth rollout continues.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Niger (health centres and health posts) are staffed by nurses who deliver a minimum package of immunisation, maternal/child and curative care using predominantly paper-based patient records. Niger's national Health Management Information System is built on DHIS2, but this operates as an aggregate reporting platform fed by facility paper tallies rather than a point-of-care electronic health record; the sector remains fragmented across more than thirty siloed digital platforms with limited facility-level integration. A community health mHealth tool for structured monitoring of children under five, newborns and mothers has been extended to four of Niger's eight regions, indicating an emerging but still partial shift toward digital data capture for specific community health functions. Poor rural electricity and connectivity, alongside a largely rural population, continue to constrain routine digital recording within clinics themselves.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations (brigades) in Niger rely on paper-based recording for case files, complaints, and incident reports, primarily through handwritten procès-verbaux (PVs). Ethnographic studies describe the process: initial data in notebooks/sheets, interviews on loose paper, pencil drafts, pen/red pen corrections, and final typing on typewriters or limited brigade computers (one per brigade, self-funded, reverts to typewriter on blackouts). Paper scarcity noted; only ~10% complaints become formal PVs. No evidence of digital recording at station level; trainings (e.g., UNODC cyber) target specialized digital forensics, not routine case management. Francophone tradition of handwritten PVs persists in rural areas without digitisation pilots/projects found. Matches broader low digitalisation in Niger's justice/police sectors.

No evidence found of digital case-recording at rural brigade level. Entirely paper confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural police and gendarmerie posts (brigades) in Niger record cases, complaints and incident reports on paper, through handwritten proces-verbaux drafted in notebooks and on loose sheets before being typed up where a typewriter or a single self-funded computer is available, reverting to manual methods during power cuts. Even the Gendarmerie Nationale's central case-file registry ('fichier central et des recherches') continues to rely on physical index cards. Donor-funded technology investment, including biometric identification equipment and computer training, is concentrated in specialised judicial-police and territorial-surveillance units rather than extended to ordinary rural brigades, which remain reliant on paper-based recording.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Niger (11,056 out of 11,638 total) record births and vital events manually on paper, producing duplicate handwritten forms: one archived locally, one sent to higher levels.CRVS Snapshot Notification and registration remain paper-based nationwide, with plans for digitization stalled by lack of electricity, internet, poor infrastructure, and climate damaging paper records. Birth registration completeness is 66.5% (2019), but vital stats compilation lags (last report 2014). Digital pilots include NRC/UNICEF equipping 81 communes (~30% of 270 total) with computers/solar to digitize 240k existing handwritten records via mobile teams in villages (2024)—not electronic point-of-service recording.NRC WURI pilot (2025) in Filingué targets 21k under-5s, digitizing existing records and training on form-filling (paper).Biometric Update UNECA notes electronic DBs only urban.UNECA Key barriers: rural infrastructure deficits. National e-gov ambitions (High Commissioner ICT since 2016) vs rural reality: paper default, donor pilots don't scale to majority facilities. Score 2: predominantly paper, some digital pilots for aggregation/digitization.

revision_notes: The original Value Code of 1 conflicted with the accompanying Comments text, which itself concluded 'Score 2: predominantly paper, some digital pilots for aggregation/digitisation' - an internal inconsistency now resolved. The originally cited crvssystems.ca country-profile page is dead (the URL now resolves to an unrelated commercial template storefront) and has been dropped. Fresher evidence (actuniger.com, May 2025, citing Niger's civil registration authority and UNICEF) confirms the 'INCI' civil-status computerisation platform is now live in 103 of Niger's 266 communes, with 40 more in progress and a national target of 87 additional communes digitised by end-2025; major declaration centres have been digitised, and mobile/biometric registration pilots (WURI, Filingue, 2025) are digitising records directly at the point of registration in some rural communes. The bulk of Niger's roughly 13,900 village-level declaration points remain paper-only, so coverage is still partial. Revised to code 2 (mostly paper, some digital) to reflect this documented partial rollout rather than a purely paper system.
revised_comments: Civil registration in most of Niger's rural registry and declaration centres remains paper-based, with births and other vital events recorded by hand and forwarded to higher administrative levels. However, the national 'INCI' civil-status computerisation platform is now operational in 103 of the country's 266 communes, with roll-out continuing to additional communes, and major declaration centres have been digitised as part of a broader civil registration reform under the 2023-2027 strategic plan. Pilot initiatives, including the World Bank-funded WURI programme in Filingue and NRC/UNICEF-supported digitisation of historical records across 81 communes, are extending direct digital capture and archive digitisation into rural areas, although the great majority of village-level declaration points continue to rely on paper forms given persistent constraints on electricity and internet access.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Niger's rural primary schools record attendance, enrollment, and grades using paper-based questionnaires filled by school heads during annual school censuses (recensement scolaire). Data is collected on paper at the school level, then controlled, entered digitally at central/regional levels, and compiled into statistical yearbooks by the Ministry of Education. EMIS exists for aggregate data production and yearbooks, with a transition plan (PTSEF 2020-2022) to strengthen it, but no evidence of digital recording or tools at rural school level. Recent projects provide computers (e.g., 38k devices via World Bank LIRE project), but these target learning environments, not data recording. Recent digital library pilots in rural schools are exceptional. Given poor infrastructure in rural areas (82% rural population), paper-based recording predominates. Score 1: entirely paper-based at facility level.

revised_comments: Niger's rural primary schools record enrolment, attendance and staffing data through the Ministry of Education's annual school census (recensement scolaire), a paper-questionnaire exercise completed by school heads and collected via regional education directorates. Data are entered centrally using the STATEDUC application and compiled into statistical yearbooks, but no digital data capture takes place at the school level itself. Given that a large majority of Niger's population lives rurally and that most rural schools lack reliable electricity or internet access, paper remains the sole means of recording data at the facility, notwithstanding recent computer provision under learning-improvement programmes such as the World Bank-funded LIRE project, which targets classroom learning rather than administrative data capture.
